dialogue.speaker: preserved-registrar
dialogue.text: You brought back a packet the Nexus could actually use. Now somebody has sent us a display board with one heading for two very different places. The ink has started to glow. We have until the visitors arrive to decide what goes on the two stands.

options.text: I’ll check the royal records first.
I’ll start with the sites marked on the coast map.

dialogue.speaker: preserved-registrar
dialogue.text: Door on the left. Follow the register beyond the burial entry. The ink is telling visitors the temple record will take them all the way to the modern catalogue. Check where that trail stops.

dialogue.speaker: preserved-registrar
dialogue.text: Door on the right. The map was folded through the middle. Unfold it before you follow the slips. The coast record asks a different question from the royal one.

dialogue.speaker: preserved-registrar
dialogue.text: The stands stay empty until we can explain both records. The royal room is to the left and the coastal room is to the right. You can leave through the south door and pick this up any time.

dialogue.speaker: preserved-registrar
dialogue.text: Our spare Lens and Thread are on the desk. Take what is missing from your kit. You can keep them if you need to return to the Nexus.

dialogue.speaker: preserved-registrar
dialogue.text: The Lens separates a date for a building from the date of a later account.

dialogue.speaker: preserved-registrar
dialogue.text: Carry the Thread to the first marker. It will leave a space where we have a gap.

dialogue.speaker: preserved-royal-keeper
dialogue.text: The name can stay on the label with its basis. You left the missing transfer open. Someone can bring us another record later without having to start the case over.

dialogue.speaker: preserved-royal-keeper
dialogue.text: One visitor saw the same name twice and asked why we need two records. Take the Lens to the temple sheet and the catalogue. The Thread begins at the burial marker. When you reach the end, give the stand a heading you can defend.

dialogue.speaker: preserved-coast-keeper
dialogue.text: Pull the site map flat. Then follow the three slips and read the context file. The old heading makes every burial here sound as if it followed the same practice. The file gives us reasons to be more careful.

dialogue.speaker: preserved-coast-keeper
dialogue.text: Now we can show why context matters. A map puts readers in the right place, and the context file tells them what preservation can and cannot show on its own.

options.text: Leave the context file open at the preservation notes.
I’ll leave the order for later.

dialogue.speaker: preserved-coast-keeper
dialogue.text: The next reader makes for the map first. A second slip sends them to the preservation notes once they find the site.

dialogue.speaker: preserved-coast-keeper
dialogue.text: Two readers stop over the preservation notes and notice the different conditions. One turns over the folder and finds the map.

dialogue.speaker: preserved-registrar
dialogue.text: We can open the display with two separate record stands, put a comparison slip between them, or open the inquiry desk while the cases wait. The gap in the royal file and the limits of the coastal record stay on the page in all three.

options.text: Open two stands. Give each record room.
Put a comparison slip between the two stands.
Hold the cases for review. Open the inquiry desk today.
I’ll look through the rooms again.

dialogue.speaker: preserved-registrar
dialogue.text: The room opens with a stand for each place. A reader stops at the gap in the royal chain. At the second stand, another asks whether preservation by itself can tell us how a burial was treated. The desk keeper is taking both requests.

dialogue.speaker: preserved-registrar
dialogue.text: Visitors walk from the comparison slip to the two records and back. A reader points to the column marked 'what we can follow' and asks where the trail goes thin in each case. The desk keeper has pulled up a chair.

dialogue.speaker: preserved-registrar
dialogue.text: The cases stay closed. The evidence desk opens. Visitors can ask why the heading was withheld and view the two record summaries while the stands wait. A reader asks where to look for the missing link.

dialogue.speaker: preserved-registrar
dialogue.text: The inquiry desk is open to the east. If you need to catch the portal, use the south door. The two rooms stay open if you want to check a record again.

dialogue.speaker: preserved-inquiry-keeper
dialogue.text: A reader copied the royal heading at the first stand. They want to check the missing link when they get home. Another read only the coastal stand. They asked where we recorded its scope. How should we leave the next reader a route to the two records?

dialogue.speaker: preserved-inquiry-keeper
dialogue.text: A visitor copied our comparison slip. Their friend took that single page to mean the two cases shared a history. Both want to know which record supports each line. How shall we keep the explanation with its source?

dialogue.speaker: preserved-inquiry-keeper
dialogue.text: A visitor thinks a closed case means we have no usable records. We can leave a trace of what is known and where the gap remains while the display waits. Where should that trace live?

dialogue.speaker: preserved-inquiry-keeper
dialogue.text: A desk copy can hold the whole reference trail. Short notes at each record can travel with a quick copy. This room has time to prepare one first.

options.text: File a traceable copy at the inquiry desk.
Clip the limits and references to the relevant records.

dialogue.speaker: preserved-inquiry-keeper
dialogue.text: A reader opens the desk copy and follows the two references in order. At the Nexus, a second copy will sit beside the return door for people who miss this room.

dialogue.speaker: preserved-inquiry-keeper
dialogue.text: A reader takes away a reference slip with the gap still marked. The next copy is going to the Nexus, where someone can find it beside the return door.

dialogue.speaker: preserved-inquiry-keeper
dialogue.text: A proof sheet for the excavation case has a date, a doorway and an empty space where the workers’ names could go. A first journal entry, a later study and the archive’s account of the workforce have arrived. We can put one claim at the top, with the other records below.

options.text: Lead with the named foremen. Leave other names open.
Lead with a dated trail from the journal to the later note.
Leave the proof on the desk.

dialogue.speaker: preserved-inquiry-keeper
dialogue.text: The foremen’s names have room on the proof. A reader asks whose names the archive did not keep. The dated documents are below the heading, with spaces for what they cannot settle.

dialogue.speaker: preserved-inquiry-keeper
dialogue.text: The note sits later on the trail than the journal. A reader points to the gap between when a record was made and when its subject happened. The workforce record stays next to the dates, with the four names in view.

missions.title: The Missing Transfer
missions.knowledgeQuestion: How can a public record name what it knows and still leave room for a missing link?

objectives.title: Hear the registrar’s plan for the two stands.
Trace the royal catalogue and repair the heading in the royal room.
Compare the site map and context file in the coastal room.
Return to the registrar and decide how to open the display.

missions.title: Room for a Reply
missions.knowledgeQuestion: What helps a reader check a claim after it leaves the room?

objectives.title: Take the reader’s request at the inquiry desk.

missions.title: Names on the Proof
missions.knowledgeQuestion: What can the date and author of a record tell us about whose story survives?

objectives.title: Inspect the excavation files and use the Lens on the journal and the later note.
Put a lead on the excavation proof sheet.

threads.title: The custody trail

nodes.label: Burial record
nodes.text: Pin the burial reference from the catalogue. The temple sheet can help place the reign. It cannot follow the later moves.

nodes.label: A later location
nodes.text: Thread the record toward Deir el-Bahari. The summary gives a later place, with room between the two entries.

nodes.label: Museum catalogue
nodes.text: The museum uses the attribution Ramesses II. Keep its name with the custody history and the catalogue that reports it.

gap.text: No transfer slip fills this space in the copy we have. Leave it open without tearing either endpoint off the line.

threads.limit: These stops follow a museum summary. We have not independently verified each transfer.

threads.title: The site and context trail

nodes.label: The site map
nodes.text: Start with the places registered in the map. A label for one coast still needs a named site.

nodes.label: Conditions and practice
nodes.text: Follow the slip to the context file. The record describes more than one way preservation could occur. Check which process the record can actually support.

nodes.label: The evidence in place
nodes.text: Clip the site and the file together. Similar preservation can leave very different histories behind it.

gap.text: This file cannot recover a particular person's wishes or every detail of a burial.

threads.limit: Comparison starts with the evidence at each place. A resemblance cannot establish a shared practice.

labelKits.title: The royal records heading
labelKits.oldLabel: A NAME PROVED BY THE TEMPLE

legends.subject: Record to put first
legends.limit: Note to keep beside the heading
legends.intro: The proof still says the temple settles the whole trail. Pin a heading to a record that can carry it. You can leave a note where the trail goes quiet.

subjects.text: The museum's record for Ramesses II

criteria.text: A monument linked to the reign
A name with a reported custody history
The temple proves every link in the custody chain

limits.text: Some transfer steps are missing from this record.
The temple and the later catalogue tell different parts of the story.

supports.subject: temple
supports.heard: A visitor follows the heading to the temple sheet and asks where the later records begin.

supports.subject: catalogue
supports.heard: The reader keeps the museum attribution beside the known locations and the missing transfer.

supports.subject: temple
supports.weak: A visitor traces a straight line from the temple sheet to the catalogue. There is no transfer record in the space where the line crosses.

weak.noSupport: The gold lights up the space where the heading needs a record.
weak.tooStrong: A reader follows the title farther than the record can take them. The gold catches on the missing link.

hints.text: Someone has set out two empty stands in the Cold Store.
The desk faces the two north doors.
Speak to Registrar Aster in the middle of the hall.
At the desk, take either starting route. The other room stays open.
A building and a museum file can have the same name on them.
Look for the temple sheet and the custody file in the left room.
After inspecting them, follow the Thread from the burial marker to the catalogue marker.
At the heading stand, use the temple record for a monument claim or the museum record for the custody claim.
Start by finding out which coast the file describes.
The right room has a map and a context file.
Inspect both. Follow the site marker, conditions marker and context marker in that order.
Keep the two preservation contexts separate. You can show either record first when the keeper asks.
Both rooms leave something a visitor can check.
Use the passage back to the Cold Store after following both trails.
Speak to Aster. The space between the stands can hold a comparison, or they can stand apart.
Choose separate records, a paired display, or an open review desk with the cases held.
Someone is asking where the heading came from.
Go to the inquiry room east of the Cold Store.
Talk to the keeper by the desk and listen to the visitor’s request.
Leave a full reference copy at the desk or clip individual references to the relevant records.
The inquiry room holds another set of records.
Find the journal, the later note, and the account of the workforce.
Inspect all three. Put the Lens on the journal and the later note.
The Lens shows when each record was made. It leaves earlier events open.
The heading at the top catches the eye first.
Read the proof sheet near the files.
Choose which part of the record visitors should see first.
The names can lead, or the two dated documents can lead. The other record stays on the proof.

journal.text: The temple sheet and custody file carry different claims. The Thread left room for a transfer we could not follow.
The sites and conditions made a difference to what we could infer from the coastal record.
We opened the room with a way to check each record. The same evidence can meet different readers in different forms.
We left a route from the public display to the record that could support it.

moments.did: Left a route to the records for readers who missed the display.
moments.prompt: Whose route to the record changed because of what you left?
